target_customer: Online marketplaces, social apps and e-commerce sites that suffer spam, scams, harassment and payment fraud
problem: Platforms needed to automatically classify user events and stop bad actors at scale without building fraud systems in house.
business_model: B2B SaaS and API for trust and safety
product_category: Trust and safety, fraud and abuse detection

founders.name: Pete Hunt
founders.background_notes: Led Instagram's web team, built business analytics, helped open source React.

founders.name: Julian Tempelsman
founders.background_notes: Worked on Gmail spam and abuse and Google Wallet anti-fraud.

founders.name: Josh Yudaken
founders.background_notes: Coverage describes the founders as ex Facebook, Instagram and Google engineers.

exit.reason: Twitter said it bought Smyte for talent and IP; customer API was shut off soon after

technical_complexity.rationale: Real time classification of event streams across spam, abuse and payment fraud needed ML and low latency infrastructure, built by ex big tech anti-abuse engineers.

defensibility.rationale: Pooled signals across customers and deep integration into event pipelines raised switching costs, but larger fraud vendors existed.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Twitter acquired it in June 2018 and disabled the customer API within about 30 minutes of the announcement.

market_need_then: Marketplaces and social apps faced growing spam, scams and harassment; customers reported by The Register included npm, TaskRabbit and Zendesk.

branding.domain_note: Used smyte.com; the domain later lapsed to an unrelated placeholder directory site.

identity.voice_and_tone: Combative trust and safety language about bad actors; one outlet headline framed it as getting biblical on bad actors

branding.community_and_virality: Press puns on the name when Twitter bought it (Twitter wants to Smyte trolls), but no community evidence found.

brand_strength.rationale: Memorable pun friendly spelling of smite drew headline wordplay, but it was a B2B infrastructure brand with little public footprint.

pivots.from: Spam and abuse blocking for social apps and marketplaces
pivots.why: Coverage notes its focus shifted toward anti-fraud applications

outcome_analysis: Smyte had unusually relevant founders from Google, Facebook and Instagram anti-abuse work, raised about 6.25 million dollars across a 2015 seed and 2017 Series A, and sold to Twitter in June 2018 for undisclosed terms. Twitter wanted the talent and IP, not the revenue, and cut off customers immediately, so it ended as a talent driven exit rather than a scaled independent business.
notes: smyte.com now shows an unrelated placeholder software directory (dead for the original business). Seed reported as $2.25M by TechCrunch and $2M elsewhere. Cloudflare, MaxMind and Castle.io were named as partial competitors in 2017 coverage, not dated to founding, so not listed. Name origin and logo not found; trademark first use June 2015. Audit fix: General Catalyst is added to the seed investors from StartupIntros, a single database whose investor table for Smyte lists 16 names without round labels, so it is unverified. The Sift Science competitor was removed because its only source was a Hacker News mirror (grivy.duckdns.org) and no dated primary source for Sift as a Smyte competitor in mid-2015 was found; Sift Science launched in March 2013 with 5.5M in funding (TechCrunch 2013-03-19), but no source ties it to Smyte as of June 2015 beyond a Smyte comment on that thread.
